verses.text: Jehoash began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah of Beersheba.
Jehoash did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes all his days in which Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.

Jehoash said to the priests, “All the money of the holy things that is brought into Yahweh’s house, in current money, the money of the people for whom each man is evaluated,  and all the money that it comes into any man’s heart to bring into Yahweh’s house,
let the priests take it to them, each man from his donor; and they shall repair the damage to the house, wherever any damage is found.”
But it was so, that in the twenty-third year of king Jehoash the priests had not repaired the damage to the house.

Then king Jehoash called for Jehoiada the priest, and for the other priests, and said to them, “Why don’t you repair the damage to the house? Now therefore take no more money from your treasurers, but deliver it for repair of the damage to the house.”
The priests consented that they should take no more money from the people, and not repair the damage to the house.

But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one comes into Yahweh’s house; and the priests who kept the threshold put all the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house into it.
When they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king’s scribe and the high priest came up, and they put it in bags and counted the money that was found in Yahweh’s house.

They gave the money that was weighed out into the hands of those who did the work, who had the oversight of Yahweh’s house; and they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders, who worked on Yahweh’s house,
and to the masons and the stone cutters, and for buying timber and cut stone to repair the damage to Yahweh’s house, and for all that was laid out for the house to repair it.
But there were not made for Yahweh’s house cups of silver, snuffers, basins, trumpets, any vessels of gold, or vessels of silver, of the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house;
for they gave that to those who did the work, and repaired Yahweh’s house with it.
Moreover they didn’t demand an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to give to those who did the work; for they dealt faithfully.
The money for the trespass offerings, and the money for the sin offerings was not brought into Yahweh’s house. It was the priests’.
Then Hazael king of Syria went up, and fought against Gath, and took it; and Hazael set his face to go up to Jerusalem.

Jehoash king of Judah took all the holy things that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah, his fathers, kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own holy things, and all the gold that was found in the treasures of Yahweh’s house, and of the king’s house, and sent it to Hazael king of Syria; and he went away from Jerusalem.
Now the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
His servants arose, and made a conspiracy, and struck Joash at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla.

For Jozacar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, struck him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in David’s city; and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Jehoash inherits a kingdom during his youth, and his mother's name is remembered alongside his. Sometimes the steadiness we need comes through a parent's quiet presence. He will reign forty years — a long harvest, long enough to see both faithfulness and its cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the turning point: Jehoash did right because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. A young man needs a wise elder, someone steady in the fear of the Lord. All the reforms that follow spring from this one choice—to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a good king cannot sweep away the old altars overnight. The high places remain, and the people still bow there. We see here the stubborn truth: our own righteousness cannot remake the hearts around us, no matter how earnestly we work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash speaks directly to the priests about the temple treasuries—money from vows, valuations, and freely given offerings. He sees what needs doing: the house of the Lord is broken and needs repair. He places the weight of stewardship on those who receive the gifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests are given clear authority: take the money each priest receives from his donors and use it to repair whatever damage appears. Responsibility paired with freedom—a trust that assumes goodwill. Will it hold?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By year twenty-three, the damage to the house has not been repaired. The money has sat in priestly hands for more than two decades while the stones cry out. Sometimes good intentions evaporate when no one stands to see them through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king confronts them directly: Why haven't you done the work? His frustration is earned. He changes the terms—no more money flows through the priests' hands. Accountability requires clarity about who answers for what.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests consent to the new arrangement. There is no record of resistance, only agreement. When power is redistributed fairly, those who held it may step aside with grace—or simply see that the work matters more than their authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiada places a chest beside the altar, on the right side as one enters the temple—visible, witnessed, secure. The threshold keepers know what comes in. Transparency itself becomes the safeguard. Small acts of honesty can redirect a whole system.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they see the chest full of money, the king's scribe and the high priest come—oversight moves into the light. They count and bag it. The change of method bears quick fruit: suddenly there is both abundance and accountability.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The money goes now to those who do the work—carpenters and builders, the hands that know how to mend stone. Stewardship finds its true purpose: the gift reaches the need. No middleman, no delay, just the Lord's house being cared for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Masons and stone cutters receive their wages. Timber and dressed stone are purchased. Every detail of repair is accounted for. There is a wholeness here—the builders are trusted to build, the suppliers to supply, each hand to its honest work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No silver cups or vessels of gold are made from this money. Nothing ornamental, nothing that catches the eye or feeds pride. All of it flows to the work of restoration—a deliberate restraint that shows where the heart truly lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They simply gave it to those who did the work and repaired the house. The sentence sits plain as stone: the money became the mended temple. This is what faithfulness looks like in its smallest, truest form.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No detailed accounting was demanded from the workers, because they dealt faithfully. Here is the paradox of trust: sometimes accountability is best served by trusting the honest to be honest. Those who mean well often prove worthy of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The money for trespass and sin offerings stays with the priests—these are their lawful portion under the temple system. Justice and order have boundaries; even the king's reforms honor the distinctions written into the law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then Hazael of Syria turns his face toward Jerusalem. The temple is being mended, but the storm clouds gather. We are never so safe in our own good work that we can forget the world's true dangers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash strips the temple treasuries and the palace gold to buy peace from Hazael. The very things his fathers had dedicated, the work just finished—given now to a foreign king. Survival sometimes demands we surrender what we hold most precious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler notes there is more to the story in the official records. We see here how one reign can build and fortify the temple, then see it stripped bare to buy tomorrow's breath. Both are part of his reign; both are written down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His servants rise and conspire, striking him at the house of Millo—a royal building, a place of power. The king who restored the temple, who brought order to the priests' chaos, falls to those closest to him. No good deed pays its own way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jozacar and Jehozabad strike their king, and he is buried in David's city—not as a dishonored assassin's victim, but among his fathers. His son Amaziah takes the throne. Faithfulness in life does not always spare us from betrayal in death, yet the Lord's memory holds longer than any conspiracy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
